repos.title: SSIO: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
repos.paper_summary: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry trains an IMU-based velocity model for a new platform without ground-truth trajectories. The method has two stages. Integration self-supervision trains a network so that the difference of its predicted body-frame velocities at the endpoints of short windows matches the bias-corrected IMU preintegrated velocity change. A static-frame regularizer suppresses spurious motion at rest. Pose graph distillation (PGD) then optimizes velocities over many windows jointly and fine-tunes the network on the resulting targets, run for one round. Across six datasets (TLIO, EuRoC, Blackbird, MIPO, GrandTour, and a humanoid), the self-supervised model has an average velocity error (AVE) within 0.07 m/s of the supervised AirIO† baseline on every dataset. For example, on TLIO AVE is 0.100 m/s versus 0.084 m/s for the baseline. The student outperforms its teacher. Limitations: the model is sensitive to constant IMU bias (0.1 m/s² bias raises AVE by 39% on TLIO) but tolerant of zero-mean noise. Tilt error from the attitude source leaks gravity into targets. Repeating PGD rounds increases error, and the method is run only once.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Inertial odometry can be trained on each new platform from its unlabeled IMU data, without ground-truth trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier self-supervised inertial methods need an extra sensor, a labeled prior, or a known dynamics model; this one needs none of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
digest_headlines.headline: Integration self-supervision matches each window's IMU-integrated velocity change, and pose graph distillation then refines the network.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Self-supervised models stay within 0.07 m/s average velocity error of the supervised baseline on all six datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis of the Learned Velocity Model
digest_headlines.headline: The student's long-horizon velocity-change error stays below its integration teacher's, and it transfers poorly across datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Constant IMU bias degrades training far more than zero-mean noise does, so bias must be corrected before training.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The student's motion model comes from averaging noisy increments, though the paper offers empirical rather than theoretical evidence for why.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers covariance propagation, training configurations, pose graph solver implementation with timing, and sample trajectories.

repos.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
repos.paper_summary: Co-Design Bench is a reference-free benchmark for coding agents that revise real users' web applications from multimodal requests. It contains 273 tasks drawn from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real coding sessions, split into Multimodal Editing (100 tasks, optional image, audio, video, or document inputs) and Repository Editing (173 tasks, coordinated multi-file changes). Each task has a runnable pre-edit app and hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria (2,331 in total). Grading is a "judge-then-refute" protocol: a fixed LLM evaluator assigns Pass, Partial, or Fail per criterion from source diffs, renders, and browser traces, then a separate LLM verifier challenges positive verdicts. Under a shared Claude Code harness, the strongest of ten endpoints (gpt-6-astra) reaches a mean strict criterion completion of 0.699 but fully completes only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints score lower on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. A limitation is that tasks evaluate a fixed request without simulated user feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench tests whether coding agents turn real users' multimodal revision requests into working application changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks cover screenshot reconstruction, predefined edits, and repository issues, but few cover compound revisions drawn from real coding sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Co-Design Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each task pairs a runnable pre-edit application with a normalized request, attachments, and hidden expert-authored criteria.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Protocol
digest_headlines.headline: A judge grades each criterion from source and browser evidence, then a separate verifier challenges positive verdicts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across ten endpoints, criterion coverage runs well ahead of complete delivery, with the top model fully passing 26.4% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench offers a shared setting for measuring complete delivery, with runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence retained.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the WebCompass execution-regime comparison, evaluator sensitivity, resource accounting, cases, dataset composition, and evaluation details.

repos.title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
repos.paper_summary: This paper measures how reasoning effort settings affect task success, cost, and agent behavior across eight proprietary and open-weight models on AIME 2026, GPQA Diamond, Terminal-Bench v2.1, and SWE-Bench Pro. Tasks and prompts are held fixed while effort varies. Higher effort often raises aggregate success but loses some tasks that lower effort solves. On tasks that every level solves, the highest level costs up to 42× the lowest. Higher effort also shifts agents toward more self-verification and, on the original SWE-Bench Pro, more reads of reference-fix commits (15.9% of tasks at low versus 75.0% at xhigh for GPT-5.6-sol). The authors test "naïve laddering," which starts at the lowest effort and escalates to the highest only after a failed external correctness check. It matches or improves success over fixed top effort for all models and benchmarks, with median cost savings of 25.3% on AIME, 41.5% on GPQA, and 15.5% on corrected SWE-Bench Pro. Limitations: each agentic task ran once per effort level, and laddering requires an external correctness check.

digest_headlines.heading: 1. Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Users choose a reasoning effort level without knowing whether more computation will help, so they cannot observe what it bought.

digest_headlines.heading: 2. Experimental setup
digest_headlines.headline: Eight models are tested across four benchmarks, varying effort within each configuration while holding tasks and harness fixed.

digest_headlines.heading: 3. Findings
digest_headlines.headline: Higher effort loses some tasks lower effort solves, raises cost on easy tasks, and shifts agents toward retrieval and verification.

digest_headlines.heading: 4. Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work reports overthinking and aggregate accuracy, but rarely audits the marginal value of effort at the task level.

digest_headlines.heading: 5. Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed effort is not cost-effective, and naïve laddering matches or improves fixed top effort where a reliable correctness check exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and inference details, experimental cost, per-setting accuracy, and repeated-run results on a software benchmark.

repos.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
repos.paper_summary: This paper proposes a framework for testing how added context changes the behavior of LLM social agents. It defines five context conditions, from minimal context to normative decision grounding, and a criterion called selective robustness: stability under meaning-preserving prompt changes, plus a prespecified directional response to changes in the social world. In a Prisoner's Dilemma-like hospital supply game run on GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra, each cell was queried ten times, and transfer probability was computed from token log-probabilities. Grounded conditions produced strong world responsiveness. Sol reached 85.9 points under descriptive grounding and 92.0 under normative grounding, with surface sensitivity of 3.7 and 3.9 points. Terra's local normative alternative-prose cell gave 89.9% transfer, versus at most 0.9% for the other surfaces. Limitations include one scenario, two models from one family, no human check of semantic equivalence, and grounded prompts that also add world detail, so salience and grounding are confounded.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Richer agent context may reduce brittleness, but context enrichment is poorly defined, so the paper proposes selective robustness for controlled tests.

digest_headlines.heading: Framework
digest_headlines.headline: Five prompt conditions are built by substitution, and selective robustness is defined by surface invariance plus prespecified world responsiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: In a hospital supply game with two models, grounded conditions produce strong world responsiveness, but Terra stays sensitive to surface form.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Outlook
digest_headlines.headline: Context construction should be treated as experimental design, though the pilot's single scenario and two models limit generalization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the AI use statement, game and prompt materials, execution details, and additional result tables.

repos.title: Scalable, Intuitive, Mixed Reality-Based Semi-Autonomous Robotic Telemanipulation for the Execution of a Fine-Grained Bimanual Task
repos.paper_summary:
This paper presents a mixed-reality semi-autonomous telemanipulation system for two UR5e arms, controlled with an Apple Vision Pro headset. It collects demonstrations for training an ACT policy on a bimanual peg-in-hole task with 1 mm tolerance. Two shared-control modes are compared with conventional telemanipulation (CT): Hybrid Telemanipulation (HT), where FoundationPose estimates object poses for autonomous grasping before the operator takes over, and Trajectory Execution Control (TEC), where the robot replays a demonstrated insertion trajectory that operator displacements adjust.

Each modality yields 30 successful demonstrations. During collection, insertion success is 0.81 (CT), 0.91 (HT), and 1.00 (TEC). Over 30 rollouts per policy, overall success is 0.03 (CT), 0.67 (HT), and 0.77 (TEC), and insertion success is 0.06, 0.74, and 0.88.

The authors name three limitations: no force feedback during contact-rich insertion, testing only with objects placed face-up, and possibly too few demonstrations, especially for CT. TEC collection was slowest (41.3 s average).

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Manual telemanipulation fatigues operators during large-scale fine-grained data collection, motivating a semi-autonomous mixed reality system.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems demand considerable operator experience, and semi-autonomous control has been tested mainly on complex assembly tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Two semi-autonomous modes automate grasping, with an operator correcting insertion by hand tracking on Apple Vision Pro.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Peg-in-hole experiments compare conventional, hybrid, and trajectory-correction modes, collecting 30 demonstrations per modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Policies trained on trajectory-correction data succeed in 23/30 rollouts, against 1/30 for conventional data.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The authors note that missing force feedback, untested flipped objects, and few demonstrations limit the system.

repos.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
repos.paper_summary: NorthCUA is a family of computer-use agent models (Nano 9B, Mini 35B, Pro 397B, all built on Qwen3.5), trained through an integrated pipeline that collects and learns from desktop and web GUI experience. The NorthCUA Harness runs tasks in isolated workspaces, records each step, and checks outcomes with task verifiers and an evaluator. The Experience Flywheel builds executable tasks and curates verified trajectories. Staged Learning applies GUI mid-training, supervised fine-tuning on verified long workflows, and joint desktop-web reinforcement learning with GRPO, using verifier outcomes as rewards. Recursive self-improvement reuses tested skills and saved verified milestones on unsolved tasks. The authors report that Pro outperforms Qwen3.8-Max and Kimi-K3 on two grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified, and that Mini surpasses Kimi-K3 on OSWorld-Verified. NorthCUA-Ultrafast, built on pre-RL Nano with a head that selects finite actions directly, completes matched successful WebArena-Verified tasks 2.3× faster on average than full generation. Stated limitations include unfamiliar software and changing interfaces, verifier coverage, sparse terminal feedback over long workflows, and indirect prompt injection.

digest_headlines.heading: 1Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA couples executable task construction, agent execution, and policy training so experience from software use feeds back into the policy.

digest_headlines.heading: 2Scope and System Overview
digest_headlines.headline: The paper separates single-step control grounding from end-to-end desktop and web tasks, each with fixed requests and completion checks.

digest_headlines.heading: 3NorthCUA Harness: Full-Lifecycle Infrastructure for Computer Use
digest_headlines.headline: The NorthCUA Harness runs each attempt through a shared runtime, long-horizon context management, outcome evaluation, and batch collection with preserved records.

digest_headlines.heading: 4Experience Flywheel: Scaling Grounding and Agentic Experience
digest_headlines.headline: The Experience Flywheel builds grounding examples and executable tasks through three construction routes, and retains progress from hard tasks via skills and milestones.

digest_headlines.heading: 5Staged Learning from Scalable GUI Experience
digest_headlines.headline: Staged Learning trains in three stages: broad GUI mid-training, verified long-horizon supervised fine-tuning, and joint desktop–web reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: 6Experiments and Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA-Pro scores 93.3% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 91.0% on OSWorld-G, the highest among systems compared in grounding.

digest_headlines.heading: 7Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA differs from prior systems by integrating decision-time input preservation and complete-attempt weighting with its harness and experience pipeline.

digest_headlines.heading: 8Limitations and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: Open limits include unfamiliar software, verifier coverage, and terminal-only feedback on long workflows.

digest_headlines.heading: 9Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: NorthCUA reports the highest open-source results across three domains and releases its three models and harness code.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation and information boundaries, grounding and task construction details, training data scale, model identities, and extended case studies.

repos.title: Evolving Agent Teams
repos.paper_summary: Evolving Agent Teams is a multi-agent framework for open-ended code optimization. A supervisor agent restructures the team's roles, coordination, and knowledge management when a run plateaus, instead of keeping a fixed configuration. A persistent file system holds a learnings document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, so each new team inherits prior results. The supervisor runs when a team finishes or on a fixed-interval cron job. Workers are Claude Code agents on Claude Opus 4.6. On GPU kernel tasks, the framework outperforms Claude Code under a matched token budget. On MLA paged decode over 47 FlashInfer-Bench workloads on H100, Claude Code plateaus at 0.44–0.51× of the FlashInfer baseline, and the evolving team reaches 0.75×. With extended budget, it reaches 1.21× mean speedup and is faster on 36 of 47 workloads. Ablations give 0.31× for a fixed four-role team and 0.28× for Codex (GPT-5.5 xhigh). Each main setting was run twice and ablations once, which limits statistical comparisons. The paper also lists a missing cost-versus-performance analysis as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing coding agents stall at local optima on expert-written GPU kernels, so the paper evolves the agent team during optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work mostly fixes agent roles or uses population search; this work restructures one team under a persistent supervisor.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A supervisor diagnoses each plateau, rewrites roles, coordination, and knowledge management, with a persistent file system carrying experience across teams.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: At matched budget the evolving team beats Claude Code on the four tasks, and reaches 1.21× on MLA decode with extra budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Evolving teams surpass FlashInfer MLA decode at 1.21× mean speedup; two runs per main setting limit statistical comparisons.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The work was done at the Sky Computing Lab, with compute support from SemiAnalysis, Amazon, AMD, and NVIDIA.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists supervisor-invented roles, a slow-start case study, extra settings, and matched-budget solo ablations.

repos.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
repos.paper_summary:
Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP) is a one-line change to multi-token prediction (MTP) training that drops the residual part of the MTP cross-entropy gradient and keeps only a KL self-distillation signal toward the model's next-token prediction (NTP) distribution. The paper splits the standard MTP gradient exactly into these two parts. It recovers the KL gradient by routing gradients straight-through from the NTP cross-entropy when teacher and student share a linear output head. This avoids vocabulary-sized logit matrices and keeps fused cross-entropy kernels usable.

Soft-MTP adds no parameters and reports no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, it gives lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding, and higher zero-shot accuracy than standard MTP at every scale, and lower MTP perplexity from 689M parameters onward. At 1.2B, it improves math and code reasoning after fine-tuning. It matches or exceeds direct KL minimization on most metrics.

Limitations: the shared output head still receives cross-entropy gradients, so only the MTP heads and shared trunk get the KL signal. Sequence sharding needs a backward exchange of hidden-state gradients at shard boundaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Standard MTP training contains a residual gradient that interferes with learning, which Soft-MTP removes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior self-distillation for MTP computes the KL explicitly or approximates it, while Soft-MTP recovers it from existing cross-entropy gradients.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Defines the next-token and multi-token cross-entropy losses for a shared linear output head.

digest_headlines.heading: Decomposing the MTP Gradient
digest_headlines.headline: The MTP cross-entropy gradient splits exactly into a KL self-distillation term and a residual term.

digest_headlines.heading: Soft Multi-Token Prediction
digest_headlines.headline: Soft-MTP sends the KL gradient through MTP heads and trunk by routing a negated residual, avoiding vocabulary-sized logits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP across 167M to 1.2B parameters on speculative decoding and downstream accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion: Practical Relevance at Frontier Scale
digest_headlines.headline: The trick needs extra communication only under sequence sharding and avoids vocabulary-sized KL tensors.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Soft-MTP is a one-line change to MTP that adds no parameters and improves NTP loss, speculative decoding and reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgements and Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The acknowledgements credit funding, inspiration from NextLat, and thanks to named collaborators.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the Soft-MTP PyTorch implementation, gradient derivations, hyperparameters, and signal-to-noise and gradient-share diagnostics.

repos.title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
repos.paper_summary: OpenTac is an open ecosystem for designing, simulating, and reading out piezoresistive tactile skins that estimate normal and shear force. Each sensor pairs a flexible PCB and piezoresistive film with an elastomeric bump strip. Sums and differences of signals across each 2×2 taxel group give normal and shear terms, which an affine calibration converts to force. OpenTac-CAD generates fabrication files and a shared manifest from a 2D outline, a developable 3D surface, or a text prompt. OpenTac-Sim is a MuJoCo FEM simulator, OpenTac-Transfer maps normal-contact fields between layouts, and OpenTac-Xampling reads sparse contacts adaptively. Across 31 fabricated boards, CAD produced zero design-rule violations and 75–93% coverage on five robot outlines. On a 4×4 patch against an OptoForce reference, R² was 0.95, 0.93, and 0.96 for Fx, Fy, and Fz. Adaptive readout on a 32×32 skin reached 1286 Hz versus 67 Hz for full scans. Limitations: the PCBs are not stretchable, surfaces must be developable, sensors show hysteresis and drift, and transfer was tested only on normal contact.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing tactile skins are hard to customize and sample slowly, so OpenTac offers a design tool, simulator, transfer, and fast readout.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems address transduction, customization, simulation, and acquisition separately; OpenTac aims to unify these from robot geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: The OpenTac Ecosystem
digest_headlines.headline: The piezoresistive skin uses a deformable bump overlay to decode shear, and four modules share one manifest file.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: All 31 fabricated boards passed design-rule checks, and the sensor's force estimates correlated with a reference sensor.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors list limits: boards are not stretchable, surfaces must be developable, sensing drifts, and sampling trades completeness for rate.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists each author's contributions, covering hardware, software, sensor characterization, policy learning, and supervision.

repos.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
repos.paper_summary: Drex is a family of four open decision models that return a probability over each question's options without autoregressive decoding. The largest, Drex Max, is a 27B dense multimodal model that reads answers from a readout head with one logit per option code, up to 255 options. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses, reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), and vision tuning. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max scores 67.52 on the public suite versus 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0. On Decision Bench v4 it reaches 94.0% accuracy, not significantly different from GPT-6 Sol and 1.6 points below Claude Opus 5.5. In a controlled ablation, RLAF adds 2.0 Decision Index points, and the consistency terms lower the top-1 flip rate from 6.3% to 4.2%. Limitations: all Drex models trail frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge benchmarks such as HLE and GPQA. Max's expected calibration error is 8.4% on questions with 6 to 20 options, and 13% of decisions with six or more options change their top option under reordering.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models read answers as option probabilities without decoding, for option sets supplied at inference time.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related work
digest_headlines.headline: The Drex models sit between option scoring, pointer networks, and calibration work, and each uses a different backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Problem formulation
digest_headlines.headline: A decision request holds a state and typed questions, and the model returns a distribution over each question's supplied options.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Pointer architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Pointer models encode the context once and score each option with a dot product between query and option-end states, with no decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Drex Max: a dense multimodal decision model
digest_headlines.headline: Drex Max removes the causal mask in full-attention layers of a 27B backbone and reads answers from a readout head over option codes.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses and reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback, with vision tuning for Max.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Experimental setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Decision Index 0.4.1, Decision Bench v4 and other suites, using Wilson intervals and exact McNemar tests on paired questions.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 Results
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover accuracy, calibration, option order, images and training stages, compared against decision-specialized and frontier chat models.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 Deployment and inference optimization
digest_headlines.headline: Shared prefill, graph capture and kernel changes cut latency, and answer-changing optimizations are accepted only within an accuracy threshold.

digest_headlines.heading: 10 Discussion and limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits: gaps to frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge, over-confidence in Max, and untested causes of its gains.

digest_headlines.heading: 11 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Drex Max leads the public Decision Index at 67.52, and its gains over the pointer models are not isolated to one design choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, question types and metrics, pointer masks, Drex Max kernel timings, deployment setups and Decision Index scoring.
